body.heading: Roles
body.introBefore: A role is a name somebody may hold, and holding one is what this service decides an ISSUANCE on. Three kinds of thing can be mapped into a role — a person, a group (so every member of it holds the role) and an APPLICATION (so a client authenticating as itself holds one, which is what a client_credentials grant is decided on, where there is no person at all). An application entry names the roles it REQUIRES in appRequiredRole, and nothing is issued for that application to somebody who holds none of them — a decision made by the XACML PDP against the policy xacml.issuancePolicy names, never by an if in an issuance site. So the reason for a refusal is a document you can read on
body.notRbacAfter: , which is the page above it in the sidebar.
body.thatOne: That one has exactly two roles, they are ordinary directory GROUPS, and what they grant is this console. This one has as many roles as you make, they live in {container}, and what they grant is being issued something.
body.twoMeet: . The two meet in one place since #303: ADMIN_READ and ADMIN_WRITE below are roles over those two groups, authorizing the management API's admin:read and admin:write. People hold them through Admin roles; an application is added to them here. And a group still grants nothing on its own, and that sentence is still true everywhere it is written. What changed is that a role may NAME a group — so adding somebody to cn=developers can now give them a role, through this register and only through it.
body.notStorable: There is nowhere to keep a role. This process has no embedded directory installed behind the register, so no role can be created. The six BUILT-IN roles below still answer — they are computed rather than stored — so an application requiring EVERYBODY still admits everybody, which is the default and means nothing is refused. There is no fallback store, deliberately: a role register that quietly lived in memory would decide things nobody could find.
body.notEnforced: Nothing is being decided. roles.enforceIssuance is OFF, so no issuance asks the PDP at all and every application admits everybody whatever its entry says. This page still records what would be asked. The switch is in Settings at the foot of this page, and it is the way back if a policy edit locks something out.
body.notGated: The XACML family is not loaded in this process. common/issuance_gate.js has no decider, so every issuance is allowed and this page is a register that nothing reads. That is the designed behaviour for a process without the engine — a smaller service rather than a broken one — and it is what npm test and the parent project's in-process Kerberos jobs run as.
body.builtInNote: Computed, in no container, and not editable. Every one of them is answered from the CONTEXT of the decision being made rather than from a store, so they have no members to list and cannot be created, renamed or deleted. {defaultRequired} is the one that matters most: an application that names no required role requires it, everybody holds it, and nothing is refused — which is exactly how this service behaved before roles existed. That is what makes this feature off by default without being absent: the machinery is always running and always visible, and narrowing an application is shortening a list rather than switching on a subsystem that has never run. The pairs are complementary ON PURPOSE and both halves exist because “everyone who did not sign in” is a thing policy authors reach for and cannot express as a negation in a XACML target.
body.madeNote: Membership, and nothing else. Each row is one entry under {container}; every column but the first is somebody who HOLDS the role. What a role is REQUIRED for is not here — that lives on the application entry that requires it and is drawn read-only further down, because it is a fact about the application rather than about the role.
body.textHint: a role, a description or a member
body.noneMade: No role has been made. Every application therefore requires {defaultRequired} and refuses nobody.
body.makeNote: The name becomes an LDAP RDN under {container} and a value in a token claim, so it is up to 64 characters of letters, digits, and . _ : @ - or a space. It may not be one of the six above: those are computed and answered first, so a stored role of the same name could never be reached.
body.name: Name
body.forApplicationTitle: Leave empty for a realm-wide role. Name an application to make a role that belongs to it alone: it is registered as {pattern}, and only a token for that application carries it.
body.memberHeading: Give a person, a group or an application a role
body.memberLead: All three are first-class members of a role here — a person, a group, and an APPLICATION holding it as itself.
body.noRoleBefore: There is no role to add anybody to yet, so this form is disabled.
body.noRoleAfter: first — the six built-in roles have no membership, because they are COMPUTED from what the party is rather than from anything anybody wrote down. That is why the Role list below is empty on a service where nobody has made one.
body.memberNameTitle: The suggestions are the applications registered in this realm. A person or a group is typed by hand and need not exist yet — this service creates an entry for any name on first sight.
body.authorizeHeading: Let a role authorize a permission
body.authorizeBefore: A scope is a request; a role is what authorizes it. A permission its resource application GATES (oauthRoleGatedPermission on the application's page) is issued only to a person or an application holding a role that names it here, and is left off the token otherwise — and a request asking for nothing else is refused invalid_scope. Name the permission as a client asks for it: the resource's oauthPermissionBaseUri followed by the name. It must be defined first. admin:read and admin:write are this service's own and are authorized by the console roles ADMIN_READ and ADMIN_WRITE alone: a person holds those through
body.authorizeAfter: , and an application by being added to them above.
body.requiringNote: The other relation, and it is edited somewhere else. An application demands roles through appRequiredRole on its own entry, which is where it is written — on the Roles tab of the application's page, as Roles a person must hold to use it, or with an ldapmodify. This table RESOLVES it for the whole realm at once: it says whether anything actually defines each role named. Only NARROWED applications are listed. Every other application in this realm requires {defaultRequired}, which everybody holds, and listing all of them would bury the ones somebody restricted on purpose.
body.unknownAfter: is not a built-in role and no entry defines it, so NOBODY can hold it and this application is issued nothing at all — which looks exactly like the application being broken. Make the role, or clear the value.
body.allDefined: Yes — every role named is defined.
body.nothingNarrowed: Nothing has been narrowed. Every application in this realm requires {defaultRequired} and refuses nobody, which is the state this service starts in.
body.previewBefore: The same call the nine issuance sites make. It goes through the embedded PEP and the PDP against the issuance policy, so a preview that agreed with the enforcement only by coincidence is impossible — which is the only reason it is worth having. Nothing is issued and nothing is recorded.
body.previewAfter: asks the same engine the other way round: an arbitrary request against the repository root, which is the policy about somebody ELSE's boundary.
body.subject: Subject
body.verdict: {decision} — {allowed, select, yes {it would be issued} other {it would be REFUSED}}.
body.builtInDeciding: The BUILT-IN issuance policy is deciding.
body.customDeciding: A policy you wrote is deciding: {name}.
body.theRule: The rule it states is the same either way — the party being authenticated must hold one of the roles the application requires — and the requirement travels in the REQUEST rather than being written into the document, which is why ONE policy decides for every application and narrowing one is editing its entry rather than editing a policy.
body.seededBefore: Nothing is seeded and there is nothing to delete. It was seeded once and the realm case killed that: ou=policies is per realm and the seed is written in the default realm at startup, so a realm created afterwards had no issuance policy and every application narrowed in it was issued NOTHING. To EDIT the rule, create a policy named {name} from the role-issuance template on
body.seededAfter: : an entry of that name overrides the built-in one.
body.overrideBefore: It is an ordinary entry under ou=policies, so the
body.overrideAfter: , ALFA, /admin-api/xacml and an ldapmodify all reach it. DELETING it puts the built-in policy back — it is an override rather than the only copy.
body.notRoot: It is not the repository ROOT and it is not sent to remote PEPs. Two questions, two documents: the root answers what a caller asks at /xacml/pdp and what every remote PEP pulls, and this answers who may be issued something HERE. Making them one document would mean editing the demo policy changed who could sign in.
body.notEvaluated: The issuance policy is not being evaluated. {why}
body.notEvaluatedRest: An application that requires only {defaultRequired} is unaffected — everybody holds it, so there was never anything to decide. An application whose entry names a role is REFUSED, and that asymmetry is deliberate: somebody deliberately asked for a restriction, and permitting because the document implementing it is missing would be a configured refusal silently not happening.
body.claimOn: Every access token, ID Token, SAML 2.0 assertion and SAML 1.1 assertion names the roles its subject holds, in {name}.
body.claimOff: The claim is OFF, so nothing carries a role.
body.claimRest:
The claim is OMITTED ENTIRELY for anybody holding no CONFIGURED role, and the six built-in ones are never in it: {defaultRequired} and ALL_AUTHENTICATED_USERS are true of almost every token this service issues, so carrying them would add two meaningless members to every token every existing client parses and tell a relying party nothing it did not know from holding the token. They exist to be REQUIRED, not to be carried.

{name} is ALSO what is looked for on the way IN: the embedded PEP reads that member out of a token a caller presented and unions what it finds with this register's own answer. That half is weaker and the policy says so in its own description — this service does not verify access tokens it did not issue, so a claim is evidence about a token rather than about a person. The role-issuance template has a parameter that leaves that arm out.
conferredBy.lead: conferred on everybody signing in through
roleEditFold.conferTitle: Every person who signs in through this client holds the role on the token it is issued, beside the roles they hold themselves.
